catalog_quote: [p.82, 3.2 Word Stress] Gugu-Badhun words have a regular primary stress on the first syllable. The only exception to this is /djibíya/ = whistler duck, where, for reasons of onomatopoeia, the stress falls on the second syllable. Stems of three or more syllables usually have a secondary stress on the third syllable. Suffixes which form a third syllable do not usually take secondary stress. [p.34, 2.2.2 Gugu-Badhun and Gudjal] Gudjal is lexically and morphologically further from Gugu-Badhun than Warungu is. It basically reflects the Gugu-Badhun phonological system but it has a full set of corresponding stops and nasals. [p.37] Only a handful of these differences suggest systematic correlations: the pairs /gamu/-/galmun/, /dami/-/dalmira/ suggest the same sort of process as is found in a number of languages in south-central Australia resulting from gemination of post-stress nasals ... while in these two Gudjal words they appear to have been preceded by /l/ [p.24, 2.1] a phonologically intact group whose words mostly or always begin with consonants, which mostly have three phonemic vowels, no fricatives, no complex syllable onsets, no word-final stops, word-stress on the first syllable and a common minimal word-structure CVCV [p.28] Mbara (aberrant) has borrowed from Ngewan (intact) and from Upper Burdekin dialects (intact) [p.30, 2.2] the term "Upper Burdekin River Dialects" refers to Warungu, Gugu-Badhun and Gudjal.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Upper Burdekin language as described from its Gugu-Badhun dialect, primary stress is fixed on the word-initial syllable; Sutton states Gudjal shares the Gugu-Badhun phonological system and treats the first syllable of Gudjal words as the stressed one ('post-stress nasals'). No Gudjal-specific stress rule is stated anywhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stems of three or more syllables usually carry secondary stress on the third syllable; a suffix forming the third syllable does not usually take secondary stress (stated for Gugu-Badhun; transcriptions e.g. [bálanò] 'moon', [búlaɹì] 'two').
new_statements.exceptions: One lexical exception in Gugu-Badhun: /djibíya/ 'whistler duck' with second-syllable stress, attributed to onomatopoeia.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule from elicited citation forms and c.11 hours of tape (Gugu-Badhun, 1970); Gudjal data = one speaker (Freddy Toomba, Palm Island 1970), lexical/morphological only. Sutton also characterises the whole 'phonologically intact' NE Queensland type, to which the Upper Burdekin dialects belong, as having 'word-stress on the first syllable' (p.24).
new_statements.identity_note: The explicit stress rule (Sutton 1973 sec. 3.2, p.82) is stated for Gugu-Badhun (Glottolog gugu1253, AUSTLANG Y128). Sutton treats Warungu (waru1264), Gugu-Badhun and Gudjal as three 'Upper Burdekin River Dialects' of one language and says Gudjal 'basically reflects the Gugu-Badhun phonological system' (p.34); his only Gudjal-specific prosodic remark is the phrase 'post-stress nasals' applied to the nasal after the first vowel of Gudjal /galmun/ 'water', /dalmira/ 'fat' (p.37), which presupposes first-syllable stress. His Gudjal data are one speaker (Freddy Toomba, Palm Island 1970; 'Toomba' Station NW of Charters Towers); a second idiolect ('Gurdjal', Ranji Pope, Charters Towers) he flags as mixed. Glottolog itself notes Sutton p.31 that Gudjal is 'too different from Warungu to be a dialect' and keeps gudj1237 separate from gugu1253, so cataloguing this under gudj1237 is an extension from the sister dialect, not a Gudjal-internal description. The same PDF resolves the gugu1253 target directly (hardlinked into with a note).
